title: Images & Dockerfiles
summary: Write Dockerfiles, build and tag images, use layers and the build cache, slim images with multi-stage builds, and push to a registry.

blocks.text: A **Dockerfile** is a text file of instructions the builder follows to create an image: commands to run, files to copy, the startup command and more. The file is named `Dockerfile` with **no extension**.

rows: Directory in the image where files are copied and commands run
Copy files from the host into the image
Run a command during the build
Environment variable a running container will use
Declares a port the image would like to expose
Default user for all subsequent instructions
Default command a container from this image runs

blocks.text:
FROM node:22-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY . .
RUN yarn install --production
CMD ["node", "./src/index.js"]
Typical order: pick a base image, install dependencies, copy in source or binaries, then configure the final image.

items: A Dockerfile must begin with `FROM` (after parser directives, comments and global `ARG`s). `ARG` is the only instruction that may come before `FROM`.
`FROM` without a tag or digest assumes `latest`. Each `FROM` starts a new build stage; `AS <name>` names it.

`RUN`, `CMD` and `ENTRYPOINT` have an **exec form** (JSON array, double quotes) and a **shell form** (plain string run via a shell). Exec form doesn't do shell variable substitution: `RUN [ "echo", "$HOME" ]` won't expand `$HOME`.
`EXPOSE` defaults to TCP (`EXPOSE 80/udp` for UDP) and **doesn't publish** the port; use `-p` or `-P` on `docker run`.
`ENV` values persist into running containers (override with `docker run --env <key>=<value>`). `ARG` values are build-time only (`--build-arg <varname>=<value>`) and aren't in the final container.
`WORKDIR` defaults to `/`; relative paths stack on the previous `WORKDIR`. Set it explicitly.
`USER` sets the user for later `RUN` instructions and for `ENTRYPOINT`/`CMD` at runtime.

blocks.text: Don't pass secrets as build arguments: they are visible in `docker history`. The reference points to `RUN --mount=type=secret` instead.
`RUN` executes at build time and commits the result. `CMD` runs nothing at build time; it records the intended command for the image.

items: Specify at least one of `CMD` or `ENTRYPOINT`. Only the **last** of each takes effect.
`ENTRYPOINT` makes the container run as an executable; override it with `docker run --entrypoint`.
`CMD` supplies defaults. Arguments after the image name in `docker run <image>` **replace CMD** and are **appended** to an exec-form `ENTRYPOINT`.
Shell-form `ENTRYPOINT` ignores `CMD` and run arguments, and runs under `/bin/sh -c`, so the executable isn't PID 1 and won't get SIGTERM from `docker stop`.
If the base image defines `CMD`, setting `ENTRYPOINT` resets `CMD` to empty.

blocks.text: Pattern to remember: exec-form `ENTRYPOINT` for the fixed executable plus exec-form `CMD` for overridable default arguments.

sections.heading: Build, tag and push
sections.sourceTitle: Build, tag, and publish an image

blocks.text: `docker build .` builds from the **build context** given as the last argument (a path or URL); the builder finds the Dockerfile and referenced files there. Without a tag the image has no name, only an ID.

items: **HOST** omitted: `docker.io` (Docker's public registry).
**PATH** on Docker Hub is `[NAMESPACE/]REPOSITORY`; no namespace means `library` (Docker Official Images).
**TAG** omitted: `latest`.
So `nginx` = `docker.io/library/nginx:latest`.

blocks.text:
docker build -t <username>/<image> .          # -t or --tag
docker image tag <username>/<image> <other-username>/<other-image>:v1
docker login
docker push <username>/<image>
Push failing with "requested access to the resource is denied"? Check you ran `docker login` and that the username in the image tag is correct.

Each layer holds filesystem changes (additions, deletions, modifications) and is immutable once created. Layers can be **reused between images**: two Python apps can share the same Python base layers, saving build time, storage and bandwidth.

items: Each downloaded layer is extracted into its own directory on the host.
Running a container builds a **union filesystem** that stacks the layers into one view, and the container's root is set to it with `chroot`.
A separate directory is added for the running container's own changes, leaving image layers untouched, so many containers can share one image.

blocks.text:
docker container commit -m "Add node" base-container node-base
docker container commit -c "CMD node app.js" -m "Add app" app-container sample-app
docker image history sample-app
`docker container commit` saves a container's changes as a new layer, but you'll rarely build images this way; a Dockerfile is the normal route.
Docker runs each instruction in order, creating a layer per instruction, and reuses a cached result when it has already run the same step. The cache is **invalidated** when:

items: The command of a `RUN` instruction changes.
Files copied by `COPY` or `ADD` change, in content or properties such as permissions.
Any earlier layer was invalidated: **every following layer is rebuilt too**.

blocks.text:
FROM node:22-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json yarn.lock ./
RUN yarn install --production
COPY . .
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "src/index.js"]

Copy the dependency manifest first, install, then `COPY . .`. A source edit then only rebuilds the last `COPY`; the install step shows as `CACHED`. Add a `.dockerignore` (e.g. containing `node_modules`) next to the Dockerfile.

A single-stage build leaves compilers and build tools in the final image, making it bulky and riskier. **Multi-stage builds** use several `FROM ... AS <stage-name>` stages: build in one, then `COPY --from=<stage>` only the artifacts into a smaller runtime image. Recommended for all application types.

FROM eclipse-temurin:21.0.8_9-jdk-jammy AS builder
WORKDIR /opt/app
COPY .mvn/ .mvn
COPY mvnw pom.xml ./
RUN ./mvnw dependency:go-offline
COPY ./src ./src
RUN ./mvnw clean install

FROM eclipse-temurin:21.0.8_9-jre-jammy AS final
WORKDIR /opt/app
EXPOSE 8080
COPY --from=builder /opt/app/target/*.jar /opt/app/*.jar
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "/opt/app/*.jar"]

items: The **last stage** is built by default.
`--target <stage>` builds a specific stage, e.g. `docker build -t spring-helloworld-builder --target builder .`
In the guide, switching from JDK to a JRE runtime stage cut the image from 880MB to 428MB.

flashcards.front: What file extension does a Dockerfile have?
flashcards.back: None. The file is just named `Dockerfile`.
Sets the path in the image where files are copied and commands are executed.

flashcards.front: Which instruction is the only one allowed before `FROM`?

flashcards.back: No. It documents the intended port. Publish with `-p` (or `-P` for all exposed ports) on `docker run`.
ENV persists into the running container. ARG is a build-time variable (`--build-arg`) not available in the final container.

flashcards.front: How are `docker run <image> <args>` arguments treated with an exec-form ENTRYPOINT?
flashcards.back: Appended after the ENTRYPOINT elements, replacing any CMD.
It runs under `/bin/sh -c`, ignores CMD and run arguments, and the executable isn't PID 1, so it doesn't receive SIGTERM from `docker stop`.

flashcards.front: What does `nginx` expand to as a full image name?
How do you add another tag to an existing image?
How does a container change files without altering image layers?
flashcards.back: A union filesystem stacks the immutable image layers and adds a directory specifically for the running container's changes.

flashcards.front: Once a build-cache layer is invalidated, what happens to later layers?
flashcards.back: All following layers are invalidated and rebuilt too.

flashcards.front: In a multi-stage build, which stage is built by default, and how do you pick another?
flashcards.back: The last stage. Use `--target <stage>` to build a different one.

flashcards.front: How does a later stage get files from an earlier one?

questions.stem: Which Dockerfile instruction sets the base image the build extends?

options.explanation: FROM <image> specifies the base image.
WORKDIR sets the working directory.
CMD sets the default container command.
USER sets the default user.

questions.stem: Adding `EXPOSE 3000` to a Dockerfile is enough to reach the app on host port 3000 without any docker run flags.

options.explanation: EXPOSE doesn't publish the port; it acts as documentation.
Use -p or -P on docker run to publish it.

questions.stem: An image has `ENTRYPOINT ["exec_entry", "p1_entry"]` and `CMD ["exec_cmd", "p1_cmd"]`. What runs with a plain `docker run <image>`?

options.explanation: Exec-form CMD supplies default arguments appended to the exec-form ENTRYPOINT.
That's what runs when there's no ENTRYPOINT.
That's the shell-form ENTRYPOINT result.
Only having neither CMD nor ENTRYPOINT is an error.

questions.stem: `docker stop` on your container always waits for the timeout instead of letting the app shut down cleanly. The Dockerfile uses `ENTRYPOINT my-server --verbose`. What's the likely cause?

options.text: Shell-form ENTRYPOINT runs under /bin/sh -c, so the app isn't PID 1 and doesn't get SIGTERM
options.explanation: The reference says shell form doesn't pass signals. Use the exec form.

options.text: The image is missing an EXPOSE instruction
options.explanation: EXPOSE is port documentation and has nothing to do with signals.

options.text: CMD must be declared before ENTRYPOINT
options.explanation: Order isn't the problem; the shell form is.
The working directory doesn't affect signal delivery.

questions.stem: Which statements about ENV and ARG are correct? Select 2.

options.text: ENV values persist in containers run from the image
options.explanation: They can be viewed with docker inspect and changed with docker run --env.

options.text: ARG values are passed at build time with --build-arg and aren't in the final container
options.explanation: ARG isn't embedded in the image.

options.text: ARG is a safe way to pass API tokens
options.explanation: Build arguments are visible in docker history; the reference advises against it.
Only ARG may precede FROM.

questions.stem: A Dockerfile contains `WORKDIR /a`, then `WORKDIR b`, then `WORKDIR c`, then `RUN pwd`. What does pwd print?

options.explanation: Relative WORKDIR paths are relative to the previous WORKDIR.
c is relative, not absolute.
pwd prints an absolute path built from the stacked WORKDIRs.
/ is only the default when no WORKDIR is set.

questions.stem: Which full image name does `nginx` resolve to?

options.explanation: Default host docker.io, namespace library, tag latest.
No namespace means library, and the default tag is latest.
The default host is docker.io, not the GitHub Container Registry.
Omitting the host means docker.io.

questions.stem: You need to publish a locally built image to Docker Hub under your account. Which steps apply? Select 3.

options.text: Tag it with your username, e.g. docker build -t <username>/<image> .
options.explanation: The name determines where the image can be pushed.
You must be authenticated before pushing.
This pushes the image's layers to the registry.
pull downloads from a registry; it's not part of publishing.

questions.stem: In `docker build .`, what does the final `.` specify?

options.text: The build context, where the builder finds the Dockerfile and referenced files
options.explanation: It is the path or URL of the build context.
Tags are set with -t or --tag.
Pushing uses docker push and the image name.
The base image comes from FROM in the Dockerfile.

questions.stem: Several containers can run from the same image because each container gets its own directory for changes while the image layers stay untouched.

options.explanation: The union filesystem adds a container-specific directory on top of the image layers.
Image layers remain unchanged, which is what allows sharing.

questions.stem: Your Dockerfile is `FROM node:22-alpine`, `WORKDIR /app`, `COPY . .`, `RUN yarn install --production`. Every HTML edit reinstalls all dependencies. Best fix?

options.text: Copy package.json and yarn.lock first, run yarn install, then COPY . .
options.explanation: The install layer then stays cached unless the dependency files change.

options.text: Add a .dockerignore containing node_modules but keep the instruction order
options.explanation: Any edit to a copied file still invalidates COPY . . and every layer after it, including the install.
EXPOSE doesn't affect caching.
File changes invalidate the cache for both COPY and ADD.

questions.stem: Which events invalidate the build cache? Select 3.

options.text: Changing the command in a RUN instruction
options.explanation: Docker detects the modification and invalidates that layer.

options.text: Changing permissions on a file copied with COPY
options.explanation: Property changes, not just content changes, invalidate the cache.
All following layers are invalidated too.

options.text: Rebuilding with no changes to the Dockerfile or source
options.explanation: That rebuild reuses cached layers.

questions.stem: In a multi-stage Dockerfile, how does the final stage get the compiled JAR from a stage named builder?

options.explanation: COPY --from copies files from an earlier stage.
FROM sets a base image; it doesn't copy individual files.
That adds a tag to an image; it doesn't move files between stages.

options.text: RUN ./mvnw clean install in the final stage
options.explanation: That would bring the build tooling back into the runtime image.

questions.stem: You want to build only the `builder` stage of a multi-stage Dockerfile. Which command?

options.explanation: --target selects the stage; otherwise the last stage is built.
Without --target the last stage (final) is built.
push uploads an image; it doesn't build.
commit saves a container's changes, not a Dockerfile stage.

questions.stem: A main benefit of multi-stage builds is a smaller final image with a reduced attack surface, because build tools stay out of it.

options.explanation: Separating build and runtime environments shrinks the image and improves security.
That's exactly the stated benefit.
